article_blocks.text: Strain Type: Hybrid
Genetics: Undisclosed Dutch hybrid
Breeder: Homegrown Fantaseeds
THC Content: 19%
CBD Content: N/A
Terpene Profile: N/A
Primary Flavors: Sweet fruit, berry, floral herbs, earth
Flowering Time (Indoor): 8 weeks
Outdoor Harvest Time: September
Indoor Yield: Moderate
Outdoor Yield: Medium
Grow Difficulty: Easy

Purple Power belongs to the period when Dutch breeders were trying to make colorful cannabis genuinely useful outdoors rather than simply visually interesting. Homegrown Fantaseeds offered the cultivar around the turn of the millennium and later cataloged it as Homegrown Purple, describing a fast-growing, quick-flowering plant that needed remarkably little attention in the garden. Its calling card was obvious at harvest: purple flowers arriving early enough for Northern European growers to finish before autumn weather became severe, accompanied by an easygoing high rather than the crushing potency associated with many later indoor hybrids. Homegrown’s own catalog called it a classic Dutch strain and specifically recommended it for beginners.

That straightforward description captures why the plant became memorable. Purple Power was not created around a laboratory THC record, dessert aroma, or complicated American pedigree. It represented practical outdoor marijuana breeding: early maturation, unusual coloration, uncomplicated cultivation, and a pleasant effect that could be enjoyed without immediately ending the day. Historical listings place Purple Power among Homegrown Fantaseeds’ catalog by 1999–2000, while later supplier lists explicitly identify Homegrown Purple as the strain formerly known as Purple Power.
Genetics and Lineage

The precise parental genetics of the original Homegrown Fantaseeds Purple Power are not publicly documented. That fact deserves emphasis because numerous modern sources attach confident formulas to the name, including Dutch Dope × Skunk #1 , Purple Haze × Skunk, Holland’s Hope × Skunk #1, and other combinations. Those may describe separate Purple Power releases or later recreations, but they are not supported by the surviving Homegrown Fantaseeds breeder catalog. The breeder instead described Homegrown Purple simply as a classic Dutch indica/sativa hybrid with indica-style growth and a perceptible sativa influence.

That incomplete family tree is typical of older European cannabis breeding. Many cultivars circulated through Amsterdam seed companies, coffeeshops, private breeders, and outdoor growers before detailed pedigree preservation became a marketing requirement. Homegrown Fantaseeds itself worked with a catalog containing older Dutch staples such as Skunk #1, K2, Northern Lights , Afghani , Californian Orange, White Widow , and other established lines, so Purple Power clearly emerged from a breeding environment dominated by classic European and imported landrace-derived genetics. The company nevertheless chose not to identify its exact parents.

Plant morphology supplies clues but not proof. The cultivar grows uniformly with the broad, controlled form commonly associated with indica-influenced marijuana, yet the smoke carries enough mental lift for Homegrown to note the sativa contribution. That combination—compact practical growth paired with a lighter, more cerebral effect—is more useful for understanding Purple Power than attaching an unverified pedigree simply because it appears frequently online.
Effects and Experience

The original breeder description centers on a “nice mellow high,” and that understated phrase separates Purple Power from the aggressively potent cultivars that dominate contemporary marketing. The experience is better understood as relaxed, buoyant, and socially comfortable than overpowering. Early effects tend to remain in the head, where mood may brighten and ordinary surroundings can feel more interesting without producing the intense racing sensation of a long-flowering tropical sativa.

Physical relaxation develops gradually underneath that mental lift. Instead of abruptly locking the consumer into a chair, the body settles while the mind remains sufficiently engaged for conversation, music, casual outdoor activity, or a quiet evening. Older grower observations also describe the cultivar as balanced and relaxing rather than heavily narcotic. That profile fits the breeder’s characterization of indica-style growth carrying recognizable sativa influence.

There is no credible original breeder THC measurement that should be assigned to every Purple Power plant. Historical material predates the modern expectation that a strain must carry a permanent cannabinoid percentage, and seed-grown cannabis can vary considerably from one phenotype and environment to another. Consumers should therefore use current batch testing whenever available. Even moderate-THC marijuana can impair memory, reaction time, coordination, and judgment, particularly when consumed quickly or in larger amounts.
Medical Benefits

Purple Power’s gentler reputation may appeal to medical marijuana patients who want cannabis that does not immediately produce heavy sedation. Relaxation, mood elevation, and a gradually calming physical effect could make this style of cultivar attractive to people managing discomfort or difficulty unwinding, but those observations remain experiential rather than clinical. No controlled study has evaluated the original Homegrown Fantaseeds strain as a treatment for a specific disease.

Cannabis research more broadly provides some relevant context. The National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health reports that cannabis or cannabinoids may offer modest benefit for some forms of chronic pain, while specific cannabinoid medicines have recognized applications for chemotherapy-related nausea and vomiting and appetite or weight loss associated with HIV/AIDS. Evidence for many other conditions remains limited, and research on sleep does not establish that marijuana reliably treats insomnia in otherwise healthy people.

A mellow reputation should not be mistaken for an absence of risk. THC-containing cannabis can cause dizziness, impaired attention, anxiety, sleepiness, and altered judgment, and cannabinoids can interact with medications. Patients seeking therapeutic effects should rely on labeled cannabinoid content, conservative dosing, and appropriate medical advice rather than assuming the historical strain name predicts a specific outcome.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

Homegrown Fantaseeds originally described the flowers as having a distinctive, almost summery fragrance without assigning a modern terpene breakdown. Historical growers tended to remember the plant more specifically for pronounced fruitiness, with some outdoor examples producing a remarkably strong ripe-fruit aroma. Sweet berry, floral vegetation, damp earth, and gentle herbal spice are consistent with the old descriptions, giving the cultivar a softer aromatic character than roadkill Skunk or fuel-heavy modern hybrids.

The flavor follows that restrained personality. Sweet fruit arrives first, sometimes suggesting dark berries or purple fruit rather than sharp citrus. Earth and fresh herbs form the middle, while mild floral and spicy tones can remain through the finish. Depending on phenotype and cure, some flowers may show more traditional Dutch cannabis funk, but the overall profile is not dominated by gasoline, pastry, or artificial-candy sweetness.

No authentic Homegrown Fantaseeds chromatography panel exists for the original release. Claims that a particular terpene such as myrcene, limonene, pinene, or caryophyllene permanently dominates Purple Power should therefore be treated cautiously unless attached to a tested modern batch. The most historically defensible description is simply sweet, fruity, earthy, floral, and herbal. Proper drying matters considerably because the lighter fruit notes disappear faster than the underlying plant and earth aromas when flowers are dried too warm or stored poorly.
Growing Information

Ease of cultivation was one of the cultivar’s strongest selling points. Homegrown Fantaseeds described Purple Power as a fast-growing, quick-flowering outdoor plant requiring very little attention and specifically called it a good choice for first-time growers. The official flowering period was approximately eight weeks, while outdoor plants were expected to finish during September—an important characteristic for northern gardens where October rain and falling temperatures can damage later cannabis varieties.

Growth leans toward indica architecture despite the plant’s hybrid effects. Stems remain manageable, the canopy develops with reasonable uniformity, and the plant does not require the elaborate height control associated with tropical sativas. Purple coloration becomes one of the most striking harvest characteristics, with flowers showing violet to deep purple tones when genetics and environmental conditions favor anthocyanin expression. Cooler late-season nights can intensify pigmentation, although color alone says nothing about potency.

Outdoor adaptability is the central reason to grow the original cultivar. Homegrown grouped it among traditional Dutch outdoor genetics capable of coping with northern European conditions and emphasized low maintenance rather than controlled-room performance. A September finish gives growers a significant head start against prolonged autumn rainfall. Basic airflow and sensible spacing remain important because no cannabis plant is completely immune to fungal pressure, particularly once flowers become mature and wet weather persists.

Indoor cultivation is possible, and the documented eight-week flowering cycle is relatively convenient, but Purple Power was historically valued far more as a garden or greenhouse plant. Growers selecting seed plants should pay attention to structure, flowering initiation, flower coloration, aroma, and resin rather than assuming every individual will behave identically. Old regular-seed populations often preserved more visible variation than highly worked modern commercial lines.

No credible original Homegrown Fantaseeds yield number survives in the breeder material examined, so presenting an exact indoor or outdoor weight would give false precision. What the breeder did emphasize was rapid growth, simplicity, outdoor reliability, and abundant purple flower formation. Those are more meaningful traits for this cultivar than a speculative grams-per-square-meter claim.

Harvest quality improves considerably with patient drying. Purple weed can look spectacular while still tasting grassy if moisture is removed too quickly. A cool, gradual dry followed by curing allows the fruity and floral components to emerge while reducing the raw chlorophyll character that can obscure an otherwise delicate old-school aroma.
FAQ
What is the genetics of Purple Power?

For the original Homegrown Fantaseeds Purple Power, later sold as Homegrown Purple, the exact parent cultivars were not disclosed in the surviving breeder catalog. Homegrown described it as an indica/sativa hybrid with typical indica growth and noticeable sativa influence. Modern sources list several conflicting pedigrees, so none should be presented as confirmed breeder lineage.
Who bred the original Purple Power?

Homegrown Fantaseeds in Amsterdam is historically associated with the original Purple Power discussed here. Cannabis literature places Purple Power in the company’s catalog around 1999–2000, and later catalog records use the name Homegrown Purple.
How long does Purple Power take to flower?

Homegrown Fantaseeds listed an indoor flowering period of approximately eight weeks. Outdoors, the breeder expected harvest during September, making the cultivar particularly useful in temperate northern climates.
Why does Purple Power turn purple?

Purple coloration comes from anthocyanin pigments expressed in the flower and surrounding plant tissue. Genetics determine whether the plant has the capacity for strong purple coloration, while cooler temperatures and other environmental factors can influence how intensely those pigments become visible.
What does Purple Power taste like?

The original cultivar is best associated with sweet fruit, berry-like notes, floral herbs, earth, and mild traditional cannabis spice. Homegrown Fantaseeds emphasized its distinctive fragrance, while historical outdoor growers also documented strong fruity aromas in mature plants.
Final Thoughts on Purple Power

Purple Power represents a kind of cannabis breeding that is increasingly easy to overlook. It was designed around the realities of outdoor European cultivation rather than maximizing THC percentages or fitting a fashionable flavor category. Homegrown Fantaseeds wanted something that grew quickly, flowered early, required relatively little intervention, produced visually distinctive purple buds, and delivered an approachable high. The breeder’s eight-week indoor schedule and September outdoor harvest show exactly how strongly practical cultivation shaped the variety.

Its uncertain pedigree is also part of the history. Multiple later marijuana strains adopted the Purple Power name, and internet sources have attached several conflicting lineages to it. The original Homegrown Fantaseeds documentation does not support any one of those named crosses. Treating the genetics as undisclosed is therefore more accurate than turning a popular secondary-source claim into breeder fact.

In the garden, the attraction is resilience and simplicity. Indica-like architecture keeps the plant manageable, early flowering reduces exposure to deteriorating autumn weather, and the purple flowers provide the visual character suggested by the name. In the jar, sweet fruit, berries, flowers, earth, and herbs create a softer profile than modern fuel-heavy marijuana. The experience completes the old-school character with a mellow combination of mental ease and physical relaxation.
